Future scenario simulation
The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) are scenario frameworks for describing and analyzing future socio-economic development trends, which are mainly used for research in the fields of climate change, environment, resources, and policy, and are especially widely used in global climate change modelling61. The core purpose of SSP scenarios is to provide multiple socio-economic development pathways for climate change research and to help predict the impacts of climate change under different socio-economic development scenarios. To project the future rooftop PV potential, we employed a delta (change factor) method. This method scales our 2020 baseline potential based on the assumption that rooftop PV areas grow proportionally to the total rooftop areas. The future projections for global rooftop area were sourced from Joshi et al.62, where the data were generated using a machine learning model driven by SSP-specific factors. As the surface-downwelling shortwave radiation is the main cause of the variability in solar power generation, we computed average annual rooftop PV power generation using daily estimates of surface-downwelling shortwave radiation rendered by GCMs from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 6 (CMIP6). The data are obtained from the World Climate Research Program’s Working Group. By combining the five SSPs with these three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs)—RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5, our study evaluates a matrix of 15 future SSP-RCP scenarios. This combination follows the standard design of the CMIP6 framework and was deliberately chosen to systematically explore a wide range of plausible futures. We note that our analysis does not cover all possible variants, such as SSP370, which represents a future of heightened regional rivalry, and the exploration of which is beyond the scope of this study. Our scenario framework encompasses a spectrum from a sustainable, stringent mitigation future aligned with the Paris Agreement (e.g., SSP126), to a middle-of-the-road trajectory (e.g., SSP245), and a high-emission, fossil-fueled development pathway (e.g., SSP585). Within this framework, scenarios such as SSP126 and SSP245 are particularly relevant to China’s policy context and long-term carbon neutrality goals. The delta downscaling method (deviation-corrected change factor method) was further used to correct SSP and RCP scenario data from 2025 to 2050. Downscaling future scenario data of Chinese cities can be calculated as equations (14) – (16):
RPA = RPA * (RAi,SSP,tn / RAi,SSP,tref) (14)
i,SSP,tn i,tref
GHI = GHI * (GIi,RCP,tn / GIi,RCP,tref) (15)
i,RCP,tn i,tref
CAP = (GHIi,RCP,tn * \eta * PR * RPAi,SSP,tn) / (CFi * h) (16)
i,SSP-RCP,tn
Where RPAi,SSP,tn refers to the projected rooftop PV area of city i in future year t under the SSP scenario. RPAi,tref is the total rooftop PV area of city i in reference year 2020. RAi,SSP,tn and RAi,SSP,tref are the rooftop areas of city i under the SSP scenario, respectively in future year t and reference year. GHIi,RCP,tn refers to the projected annual solar radiation of city i in future year t under the RCP scenario. GHIi,tref is the annual solar radiation of city i in reference year. GIi,RCP,tn and GIi,RCP,tref are the annual radiation of city i under the RCP scenario, respectively in future year t and reference year. CAPi,SSP-RCP,tn is the rooftop PV capacity potential of city i in future year t under the combined SSP and RCP scenario. CFi is the capacity factor of city i, which is shown in Supplementary Fig. 13. h denotes the annual hours.

To represent the future evolution of provincial power generation mix, we adopted optimized generation structures for 2025–2050 derived from a province-level energy modeling framework63. Based on the dynamic mixes, we calculated the carbon, water, and land intensities of provincial power generation. The assessment covered a full portfolio of generation technologies, including coal, gas, biomass, hydro, wind, solar, and nuclear power. In our research, with a specific focus on wind and solar as the key drivers of decarbonization, the onshore wind and utility-scale PV in the power mix were selected as the representative technologies to reflect technological advancement, while the life cycle intensities of other generation technologies were held constant. To be specific, we estimated the future annual generation of wind and utility-scale PV based on technology-specific drivers (improving capacity factors for wind64, and changing solar radiation and conversion efficiency for PV). We further updated the future life cycle inventories of wind and utility-scale PV, including embodied material impact decrease and recycling rate increase. See Supplementary Fig. 14 for the details.

Concurrently, we developed a dynamic life cycle inventory framework specifically for rooftop PV systems to simulate the distinct technological trajectories. Key assumptions were as follows: recycling rates for major module materials (limestone, soda, silica sand, copper, and aluminum) were assumed to increase at a conservative annual rate of 2%, reflecting progressive material recovery policies; the embodied environmental intensities of non-electrical components, including glass, aluminum frames, and mounting brackets, were assumed to decline by 1% per year, representing cleaner material production65; PV module degradation was incorporated, with a rate of 2% in the first year and 0.55% annually thereafter, based on field investigation; and PV module conversion efficiency was projected to improve at an annual rate of 0.35%, starting from a 2020 baseline of 16%, according to the Energy Research Institute of the National Development and Reform Commission of China66. Notably, throughout the whole life cycle, the electricity for rooftop PV comes from the evolving provincial power generation mix from 2025 to 2050. To capture parametric uncertainties, we also implemented a Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations) on critical variables, including cleaning water usage, solar irradiation, and provincial grid mix.

We further evaluated future rooftop PV deployment schemes that incorporate economic feasibility to reflect realistic deployment constraints. Specifically, the 349 cities were ranked by their LCOE from low to high and divided into four quartiles. Development rates of 80%, 60%, 30%, and 10% were assigned to the first through fourth quartiles, respectively, capturing the decreasing likelihood of deployment with lower economic attractiveness. The economically adjusted rooftop PV potential for each city and SSP pathway was then calculated by multiplying the maximum technical potential by the corresponding development rate. Based on the city-level rooftop PV deployment schemes, we quantified the future carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV. Simulation results are reported using the median (50th percentile) as the central estimate, with 95% confidence intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) provided to characterize the uncertainty bounds. To further evaluate the broader significance of the carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV, we benchmarked them against China’s national shares of planetary boundaries67, thereby assessing the extent to which rooftop PV can contribute to mitigating environmental pressures within safe operating limits.

This study presents a systematic evaluation of the carbon mitigation, water savings, and land occupation benefits of rooftop
PV systems at the city scale across China. It integrates LCA, SSP scenario modeling, and machine learning. The study
addresses a timely issue using an interdisciplinary methodological framework. However, the
manuscript currently suffers
from substantial issues regarding the applicability of key methodological assumptions, the completeness of result
interpretation, and the reliability and transparency of data sources. These limitations may lead to overstatements or even
misinterpretations of the conclusions. The manuscript cannot be considered for publication unless the authors resolve the
following major concerns:
1. Data foundation and model training
(1) The authors mention using web-scraping techniques to collect building data from 124 cities, but the original data sources,
interpretation methods, spatial resolution, or labeling accuracy are not disclosed. The spatial distribution of the sampled
cities is also not provided.
(2) A machine learning model trained on the 124-city sample is used to extrapolate rooftop PV deployment potential to 349
cities. However, the authors do not report the generalization error across different geographic or urban typologies. It is
recommended to provide spatially resolved model performance metrics and identify areas with large uncertainties to improve
the credibility of extrapolated results.
2. Assessment of carbon, water, and land benefits
(3) The manuscript notes that previous studies may have overestimated rooftop PV carbon mitigation by 13–23% due to
using only operational emissions. While the authors adopt an LCA framework to estimate the lifecycle carbon, water, and
land footprints of rooftop PV, the grid-side comparison benchmark (i.e., CE_grid,z,t) is based solely on direct emissions from
electricity generation, without incorporating the full lifecycle emissions of different energy types. This inconsistency in system
boundaries introduces systematic bias. How do the lifecycle emissions of rooftop PV compare with those of conventional
energy sources under a consistent framework? The authors are advised to align system boundaries or at least conduct
sensitivity analyses to quantify the impact of this assumption.
(4) For estimating water and land savings, the authors compare provincial average grid water and land intensity with city-
level rooftop PV indicators. However, electricity generation is spatially heterogeneous within provinces, and interprovincial
power transfers are common. Comparing provincial averages directly with city-scale rooftop PV values introduces potential
spatial mismatches. The authors should clarify how such uncertainty is addressed.
3. Future scenario modeling
(5) The manuscript reports that in certain cities, rooftop PV may increase emissions in the future, due to faster
decarbonization of the grid than the carbon savings from rooftop PV systems. While future grid structures are projected under
SSP-based scenarios, the rooftop PV lifecycle parameters (carbon, water, and land) remain static. No explanation is given
as to whether rooftop PV parameters are assumed to evolve over time (e.g., improved module efficiency, cleaner
manufacturing). The authors are encouraged to introduce at least two technology development paths (e.g., “no improvement”
vs. “technical advancement”) and assess their impact on the conclusions. Without this, the “net-negative mitigation” claim
may be overstated.
(6) Although the authors evaluate both the environmental benefits (carbon, water, land) and economic feasibility (e.g., LCOE,
investment payback period) of rooftop PV deployment, these assessments are conducted in isolation. The scenario
modeling assumes widespread rooftop PV deployment regardless of regional differences in economic feasibility. It is
recommended that the authors integrate economic feasibility as a constraint in the future scenario simulations, to construct a
more realistic and policy-relevant cost–benefit trade-off framework.

### Reviewer 2

This study offers an impressive city-scale assessment of rooftop-PV deployment and its energy–carbon–water–land nexus
for 349 Chinese cities, weaving together machine-learning roof-area estimates, a seven-stage life-cycle assessment (LCA),
and SSP–RCP scenario modeling through 2050. Its most striking insight is that once provincial grids decarbonize, rooftop
PV can raise net-life-cycle CO₂ in several hydro-dominated provinces while water- and land-saving benefits continue to
grow. The work, therefore, moves the debate beyond “more solar = less carbon,” reminding policy-makers that the value
proposition for distributed PV will shift from carbon to other resource metrics. The geographic resolution and multi-
dimensional framing add real value to the literature. The methods are generally sound and rest on reputable data sets
(CMIP6, Ecoinvent v3.7, Feng et al. 2014). Still, several simplifying assumptions —static PV parameters, deterministic
outputs, a theoretical self-sufficiency index, and full-roof uptake—limit operational credibility. Addressing the issues below
will strengthen the science and its usefulness to decision-makers.
Major comments
1. UESS is calculated as annual PV generation divided by annual demand, with no modeling of hourly load mismatch,
storage, or distribution network hosting limits. Please clarify the metric’s theoretical nature and discuss how diurnal
mismatch and grid hosting limits could affect the headline results and policy relevance. Current wording risks being
interpreted as operational autonomy.
2. Embodied-carbon factors: one size does not fit all. The “negative-mitigation” result rests on a single national LCA profile
for PV modules and the balance-of-system. Please discuss if region-specific module footprints could alter the conclusion.
3. Module efficiency is fixed at 15 %, degradation is ignored, and life-cycle inputs stay constant. Model at least one learning-
curve scenario (higher efficiency, lower embodied CO₂, improved recycling) or bound the likely impact qualitatively.
4. Roof-area prediction error, CMIP6 climate spread, and future grid-mix assumptions are all uncertain, yet outputs are
deterministic. Provide Monte-Carlo bands or simple high/low envelopes for key results such as pay-back times and nexus
benefits. Robustness cannot be judged otherwise.
5. Assumption of full rooftop deployment: The core scenarios presume near-complete utilization of all “suitable” roofs. Add
illustrative adoption rates (e.g., 30 % and 60 %) or explicitly discuss socio-economic barriers so readers can judge the
resilience of the conclusions.
6. Multi-gigawatt rooftop PV in dense urban networks will face hosting-capacity limits and potential curtailment. Include a
concise subsection summarising Chinese distribution-code limits, storage targets, and typical curtailment ranges to ground
the findings in operational reality.
7. Explain why specific SSP–RCP pairs were chosen, note which combinations are most policy-relevant for China, and
discuss scenarios not covered. Readers need to know what scenarios do—and do not—cover.
8. Uniform water- and land-use factors: Cleaning frequency, dry-clean technologies, and the urban opportunity cost of roof
space vary widely. Flag these caveats or add a sensitivity range to avoid over-generalization across diverse climates.
Minor comments
1. Figures – add axis labels, R² / p-values where regression lines are shown, and uncertainty ribbons where feasible.
2. Terminology – use “theoretical self-sufficiency” consistently; distinguish “built-up” from “hinterland” throughout.
3. Units check – land-occupation values are reported as 33.8–64.3 ha kWh⁻¹, which seems dimensionally improbable;
please verify units (perhaps ha GWh⁻¹).
4. Discussion – the section linking technical findings to policy is excellent; retain this strength.

## Paper

## Abstract

Rooftop photovoltaics are widely recognized for their carbon mitigation benefits, yet uncertainties persist regarding their future dynamics and broader impacts on water and land. Here we develop a city-level integrated framework to quantify rooftop photovoltaics potential across 349 Chinese cities, and evaluate evolving carbon-water-land tradeoffs under shared socioeconomic and representative concentration pathways. By 2050, projections across 15 combined scenarios indicate China’s rooftop photovoltaic areas will increase by 9.2 to 34.8 percent relative to 2020 levels. Installed capacity ranges from 7.19 to 9.05 terawatts in 2050, expanding rapidly in eastern coastal cities. Under a moderate socioeconomic and climate scenario, the national carbon mitigation benefits peak during 2035 to 2040, accumulating 2.04 to 2.18 gigatons of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2050. In contrast, the water and land saving benefits continue to rise, reaching 16.5 to 17.4 cubic kilometers and 281 to 297 thousand square kilometers by 2050. These findings underscore the critical need for multidimensional planning to optimize future sustainable photovoltaics deployment.

---

## Introduction

Cities are pivotal engines of future population growth, innovation, and economic opportunity worldwide1. Yet, a significant share of global urban areas still faces acute energy shortages, with approximately 760 million people globally lacking access to electricity in 2023, predominantly in developing countries and emerging economies2. Conventional power generation systems, often located far from demand centers3, thus remain out of sight and mind for the public. Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems, a hallmark of distributed energy, utilize idle urban rooftop spaces to enable localized power generation4, which can offer remarkable spatial adaptability and energy self-sufficiency5,6. Compared with centralized power plants, rooftop PV not only reduces long-distance transmission losses by an estimated 6–8%7 but minimizes land requirements, making it an effective strategy for alleviating urban land use conflicts and enhancing the resilience of energy systems8,9. Globally, the development potential of rooftop resources is vast. Estimates suggest that rooftops cover 200,000 km2 of the planet’s 13 million km2 land surface, with Asia accounting for a substantial share10. In China alone, the total rooftop area across 354 cities reached 66,000 km2 by 2020, signaling enormous untapped capacity for rooftop PV deployment11.

Amid intensifying global warming, the carbon mitigation benefits of rooftop PV have garnered widespread attention12. Research has largely centered on carbon emission mitigation during the operational phase13–18. Yet recent insights suggest that ignoring emissions across the full life cycle—from raw material extraction through manufacturing, transport, installation, and maintenance—may inflate the perceived climate benefits of rooftop PV19–22. Moreover, a singular focus on carbon mitigation may obscure the multidimensional impacts of rooftop PV and miss opportunities to embrace broader sustainability development goal (SDG). Recognizing the close interlinkages between energy (SDG7), carbon (SDG13), water (SDG6), and land (SDG15)23,24, urban policymakers should integrate a holistic view that considers not just energy generation, but also the indirect resource consumption (e.g., materials) and its cascading implications for water and land systems25.

In terms of water use, though rooftop PV consumes water during material production and operation26,27, its life cycle water footprint remains lower than that of fossil fuel-based generation mix. In California, for example, residential rooftop PV saves an average of 200 cubic meters of water annually, around 60% of the typical American household’s consumption28. Regarding direct land use, rooftop PV capitalizes on existing urban building landscapes, and avoids the need for additional ground space29,30. While utility-scale PV stations conversely depend on vast tracts of farmland, grassland, or ecological zones, potentially triggering land use conflicts and ecological pressures31–33. Coal-based power compounds this issue with extensive land demands for mining, storage, and transmission34. Seen from the entire lifespan, rooftop PV entails indirect land occupation that amounts to only a fraction of that associated with coal-fired power26,35. Nevertheless, whether rooftop PV consistently offers land saving advantages over power generation mix warrants further quantification.

As ambitious calls for net-zero power systems grow, the large-scale integration of renewables promises to sharply lower carbon emission factors of power generation mix36–38. However, the carbon mitigation benefit of rooftop PV will inherently change, when considering the generation mix decarbonizes and rooftop PV’s technological advancement. Meanwhile, little is known about the future performance of rooftop PV regarding water and land dimensions. These uncertainties complicate efforts to evaluate the energy-carbon-water-land tradeoffs between rooftop PV and power generation mix, particularly under varying future socio-economic-climate trajectories. Bridging these knowledge gaps can help refine contributions of rooftop PV to the SDGs and inform tailored, evidence-based urban energy strategies.

To tackle these challenges, we constructed a city-level methodological framework for quantifying the rooftop PV’s tradeoffs (Fig. 1), blending machine learning, life cycle assessment, and forward-looking scenario simulations. The model can map out city-level rooftop PV potential and quantify the associated carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving, projecting their evolutionary trends from 2025 to 2050. By weaving in socio-economic-climate scenarios, provincial generation mix evolution, and PV technological advancement from 2025 onward, we illuminate the nexus dynamics of rooftop PV across multiple dimensions. Applied to 349 Chinese cities, we uncover the notable spatial variations of rooftop PV in tradeoffs against local power generation mix. This study equips stakeholders with a view of rooftop PV’s untapped value and arms urban decision-makers with context-specific evidence for designing effective, locally tailored energy transitions.

---

## Results

Rooftop photovoltaic potential within city boundaries
This study developed a machine learning model to predict the rooftop PV potential across 349 Chinese cities, including built-up areas and hinterlands within city administrative boundaries. To assess the robustness and generalizability, the cross-validation procedure was applied to subsets of data stratified by China’s seven geographical regions and by city-level gross domestic product (GDP) classifications (see Methods and Supplementary Figs. 1–2). We estimated that China possesses a total of 33,290 km2 of rooftop PV potential across 349 cities. However, this resource is distributed unevenly, with the majority located in densely built and highly urbanized eastern regions. At the city scale, rooftop PV potential varies substantially, ranging from 2.4 km2 in Wuzhishan to 533 km2 in Chongqing. The leading cities include Chongqing, Weifang, Linyi, Shijiazhuang, and Baoding (Fig. 2a). Comparing built-up areas to hinterlands, Shenzhen, Shantou, and Wuzhishan offer higher rooftop PV potential in built-up areas. While the other 99% of cities exhibit greater potential in hinterlands, ranging from 1.2 to 68 times higher than built-up areas, which is consistent across all provinces (Supplementary Fig. 6). Shandong province exemplifies this spatial structure, as its extensive rooftop areas in hinterlands, combined with strong policy support, have enabled it to emerge as a national leader in distributed rooftop PV development.

We compared the rooftop PV generation with total electricity demand in city administrative boundaries (Supplementary Fig. 7) to evaluate the theoretical urban electricity self-sufficiency (UESS). The UESS ranges from 16% to 417% (Supplementary Fig. 8a). It was further found that 87% of cities (302 of 349), primarily concentrated east of the Hu Huanyong Line (Fig. 2b), could theoretically generate more electricity than they consume. In built-up areas, rooftop PV can meet a small portion of demand, ranging from 0.8% to 58.5% (Fig. 2c). Conversely, rooftop PV in hinterland can satisfy 11%–403% of city electricity demand (Fig. 2d), and 82% of cities (286 of 349) can fully achieve the electricity self-sufficiency.

Our assessment of China’s five largest cities by GDP (Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Chongqing, and Guangzhou) shows significant variation in the potential for rooftop PV to meet local electricity demand (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Among them, Chongqing exhibits the greatest theoretical self-sufficiency (134.5%), with generation capacity far exceeding its demand. This is largely driven by its hinterland (126.8%), while its built-up area contributes only 7.7%. In contrast, Shenzhen (53.8% total) follows a built-up area–dominated mode, where 40.1% of potential arises from the urban core compared to only 13.7% from the hinterland, consistent with its compact urban form. For Shanghai, Beijing, and Guangzhou, they rely significantly on their hinterlands. Shanghai has a total UESS of 58.2%, with 41.0% coming from the hinterland and 17.2% from the built-up area. In Beijing and Guangzhou, built-up areas contribute around 18.5% and 12.8%, respectively, to their total UESS, while the hinterlands provide the larger share. These profiles underscore the importance of aligning rooftop PV deployment strategies with the spatial configurations and morphological characteristics of different megacities.

Energy-carbon-water-land nexus of rooftop photovoltaics
By integrating local solar irradiation, PV conversion efficiency, and performance ratio, we evaluated the rooftop PV generation potential across cities (Fig. 3a). Since rooftop PV systems offer a viable alternative to local power generation mix, the comparison between rooftop PV and generation mix is crucial to determine the practical benefits and limitations of each. We defined the life cycle system boundaries for rooftop PV, encompassing material production, manufacturing, transportation, installation, operation, decommissioning, disposal, and recycling (Supplementary Fig. 9). We included the direct impacts (energy and water input, carbon emissions), and accounted for the embodied impacts (by materials and resources) of rooftop PV (Supplementary Methods). In particular, we incorporated the direct cleaning water usage during operational stage, informed by company interviews on rooftop PV practices (Supplementary Table 2), which cover diverse techniques (e.g., robots, drones, handheld brushes) with varying water intensities and cleaning frequencies. The life cycle assessment results per kilowatt-hour (kWh) indicate that rooftop PV systems generate carbon emissions (52.2–99.3 g kWh-1), and require water consumption (0.34–0.65 L kWh-1) as well as land occupation (0.0034–0.0064 m2 kWh-1). For comparison, we benchmarked the life cycle impacts of rooftop PV against the local power generation mix on a per kWh electricity basis. The life cycle carbon emission, water consumption, and land occupation of power generation mix (Supplementary Table 5) were computed based on provincial generation structures (Supplementary Table 6) and the corresponding life cycle impacts of each generation technology (see Methods for details). Our analysis reveals that rooftop PV substantially outperforms generation mix across the carbon, water, and land impact dimensions from a life cycle perspective. Specifically, for each kWh of electricity generated compared with generation mix, city-level rooftop PV in China provides median benefits of 759 g in carbon mitigation, 3.4 L in water saving, and 0.05 m2 in land saving. These benefits exhibit significant spatial heterogeneity, with city-level values ranging from 81.6–1362 g kWh-1 for carbon mitigation, 2.4–15.1 L kWh-1 for water saving, and 0.02–0.11 m2 kWh-1 for land saving.

From a carbon perspective, rooftop PV generation in provinces such as Inner Mongolia (1348–1362 g kWh-1), Jilin (1070–1076 g kWh-1), Heilongjiang (1064–1074 g kWh-1), Shanxi (1041–1049 g kWh-1), and Zhejiang (1041–1046 g kWh-1) showcase high carbon mitigation benefits (Fig. 3b). This is primarily due to the high proportion of coal power in the power structures of these provinces and the high life cycle carbon intensity of coal power generation. However, regions like Sichuan (82–124 g kWh-1) and Yunnan (100–121 g kWh-1) exhibit poor carbon mitigation benefits (Fig. 3b) and long carbon payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3a). The main reasons for this are twofold: First, these areas benefit from low-carbon generation structures dominated by hydropower, indicating that the electricity substituted by rooftop PV is already clean, which results in minimal mitigation. Second, weak solar radiation (especially for some cities in Sichuan) due to basin topography reduces the lifetime energy generation of PV systems. This effectively increases the PV system’s life cycle carbon emissions per kWh generation, diminishing its overall life cycle environmental benefits. However, Sichuan (14.9–15.1 L kWh-1), Yunnan (14.3–14.3 L kWh-1), Qinghai (11.3–11.34 L kWh-1), and Hubei (10.5–10.6 L kWh-1) exhibit the most substantial water saving benefits through rooftop PV generation (Fig. 3c), leading to the lowest water payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3b). This is because their provincial generation mixes contain a high share of hydropower, whose life cycle water consumption is comparatively large, thereby leading to greater water saving when substituted by rooftop PV. Heilongjiang and Hainan stand out for their substantial land saving benefits, with values of 0.105–0.106 m2 kWh-1 and 0.962–0.967 m2 kWh-1, respectively (Fig. 3d). This stems from the higher proportion of biomass in the power structure of these two provinces. Biomass has a greater life cycle land occupation, and thus elevate the land factors of generation mix. The rooftop PV in these regions thereby yields more pronounced land saving benefits, resulting in shorter land payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Conversely, Qinghai (0.023–0.024 m2 kWh-1), Shaanxi (0.033–0.035 m2 kWh-1), Guizhou (0.033–0.034 m2 kWh-1), Xinjiang (0.028–0.029 m2 kWh-1), and Gansu (0.0275–0.0289 m2 kWh-1) present the least significant land saving benefit (Fig. 3d) and, therefore, have longer land payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3c).

Beyond resource and environmental impacts, we evaluated the economic performance of urban rooftop PV using the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), explicitly accounting for rooftop rental costs (Supplementary Table 7) in addition to initial capital investment, operation and maintenance costs. The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of rooftop PV is estimated at 0.041–0.077 USD kWh-1 (Fig. 3e), ensuring user-side grid parity across 349 cities (Supplementary Fig. 5), that is, rooftop PV electricity costs are no higher than the retail tariffs paid by consumers. The payback periods, however, exhibit pronounced heterogeneity (Supplementary Fig. 3d), mainly driven by differences in local electricity tariffs, rooftop rents as well as PV generation. Due to low electricity tariff in Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, and low generation per unit area in Sichuan, Guizhou, and Gansu, Xinjiang (13.8–16.9 years), Inner Mongolia (11–14.5 years), Sichuan (8.4–16.2 years), Guizhou (12.9–16.9 years), Gansu (11.1–16.6 years), and parts of Shaanxi (9.7–14.4 years) require longer periods to offset their economic costs. We further examined the spatial distribution of the economic cost required per unit of benefit (based on the normalized sum of carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving) for urban rooftop PV (Fig. 3f). Gansu, Shaanxi, Guizhou, Fujian, and Guangdong challenge high costs when generating carbon-water-land benefits, while Heilongjiang, Jilin, Hebei, Yunnan, and parts of Inner Mongolia and Sichuan have low costs, driven by favorable LCOE and positive environmental performances in carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving. These heterogeneities suggest that deployment strategies should be tailored to specific regions. Areas with high benefits and low costs should prioritize the adoption of rooftop PV, while regions with high costs require policy and technological support to enhance the viability of deploying urban rooftop PV.

Future scenarios reshape rooftop photovoltaics’ nexus
Under the framework of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), we projected the expansion of China’s rooftop PV area from 2025 to 2050, based on the maximum exploitable potential. Our results indicate substantial variations in future rooftop PV expansion, with growth trajectories diverging markedly among SSPs. By 2050, the fossil-fueled development scenario (SSP5) shows the largest increase, with the national rooftop PV area reaching a median of 44,877 km2, representing a 34.8% rise (95% CI: 31.9%–37.5%) relative to 2020 levels. In contrast, the sustainability scenario (SSP1) yields the smallest increase, reaching 36,346 km2, and a 9.2% rise (95% CI: 7.3%–11.1%). The intermediate scenarios fall between these two extremes: the middle-of-the-road scenario (SSP2) results in a 24.8% increase (95% CI: 22.2%–27.3%), while the regional rivalry (SSP3) and inequality (SSP4) scenarios show moderate growth of 14.9% (95% CI: 12.3%–17.5%) and 14.5% (95% CI: 12.1%–17.1%), respectively (Fig. 4a).

We further combined the SSP-based rooftop PV area projections with radiative forcing estimates under three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs), including RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5. This integration enabled Monte Carlo simulations of China’s rooftop PV installed capacity potential from 2025 to 2050, covering 15 SSP–RCP combinations. Under the maximum rooftop PV potential, the median national installed capacity by 2050 is projected to increase by 74.4% (95% CI: 67.3%–81.6%) under the SSP185 scenario and by 119.6% (95% CI: 98.6%–141.2%) under the SSP545 scenario, corresponding to 7.19 TW (95% CI: 6.89–7.49 TW) and 9.05 TW (95% CI: 8.19–9.92 TW), respectively (Fig. 4b). Under the middle-of-the-road SSP245 pathway, the national installed capacity will to reach a median of 8.2 TW by 2050, a 103% increase (95% CI: 87.4%–119.4%) relative to year 2020 (Fig. 4b). Under the SSP245 scenario, rooftop PV generation across China’s 349 cities will increase substantially, with the national average growth reaching 87.5% by 2030 and 193.6% by 2050 relative to 2020 levels (Fig. 4c). However, this potential is highly uneven, the eastern coastal cities are primary hotspots for future rooftop PV deployment, with Shandong projected to reach 786.7 GW by 2050 (Supplementary Table 8). A broad cohort of economically developed cities or those with abundant solar resources in this region, including Huizhou, Wenzhou, Ningde, and Qingdao, consistently exhibit strong long-term potential, with projected growth rates commonly exceeding 200%. In addition, cities like Panjin (448.8%), Mianyang (406.5%), and Longyan (347.9%) are projected to see their generation increase more than four-fold, indicating significant local drivers. Whereas cities in the northwest or less-developed regions, such as Jiayuguan and Wuzhishan, show significantly more modest, though still positive, growth trajectories.

We incorporated anticipated advances in rooftop PV to project the future life cycle carbon, water, and land intensities of rooftop PV systems, including improved conversion efficiency, enhanced recycling rate, and decreased embodied impacts of key materials. These life cycle evolution of rooftop PV was integrated with provincial power generation structure optimization scenarios to assess the future dynamics among carbon, water, and land benefits. Under policy-driven constraints, coal- and gas-fired generation in the power structure is projected to peak around 2030 and 2040, respectively, while renewable penetration increases, with solar and wind power progressively dominating China’s electricity mix, complemented by hydropower, nuclear, and biomass (Supplementary Fig. 10). Within the power generation mix, the life cycle carbon, water, and land intensities of solar and wind power are projected to evolve over time, reflecting anticipated technological advancement, and the intensities of other generation technologies (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, and biomass) are assumed constant. The results indicate that the life cycle carbon intensity of rooftop PV steadily decreases with technological advancement, and the carbon intensities of power generation mix also decline due to a rising share of renewables (Supplementary Fig. 11). For water and land, however, the trajectories of provincial generation mix factors are more heterogeneous. Some provinces exhibit decreases, whereas others remain relatively stable or fluctuate depending on their generation structure (Supplementary Fig. 11). In contrast, rooftop PV shows a consistent downward trend in water and land intensities. These dynamics highlight that the relative benefits of rooftop PV are shaped jointly by PV technological advancement and generation structure evolution differences. Results show that the unit carbon mitigation benefit is projected to decrease over time, with the median value declining from 713.6 g kWh-1 in 2025 to 388 g kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). Similarly, the unit water saving benefit shows a slight downward trend, with the median decreasing from 3.9 L kWh-1 in 2025 to 3.5 L kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12b). In contrast, the unit land saving benefit demonstrates an increase, rising from 0.043 m2 kWh-1 in 2025 to 0.056 m2 kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12c), with the growing efficiency of life cycle land occupation of rooftop PV. The unit benefits and payback periods, with and without technological advancements, are additionally shown in Supplementary Fig. 12d–f.

We further developed economically-constrained deployment scenarios to reflect the possibilities of market attractiveness on city-level rooftop PV rollout. To achieve this, we ranked and grouped all 349 cities into four quartiles based on their LCOE. We then applied tiered deployment rates to these quartiles to simulate a market-driven pathway where more profitable regions are prioritized. Specifically, the deployment rates were set at 80%, 60%, 30%, and 10%, corresponding to the quartiles from the most economically attractive (lowest LCOE) to the least. The final deployment level for each city under a given SSP scenario was then determined by multiplying its maximum technical potential by its assigned quartile-specific rate. This approach allows for the evaluation of future carbon, water, and land benefits under large-scale rooftop PV development schemes. Results show that at the national scale, the carbon mitigation benefit of rooftop PV will first rise to a peak around 2035–2040 and then decline (Fig. 5a), while the water and land saving benefits will consistently increase over time (Fig. 5b&c). Under the SSP245 scenario, the carbon mitigation benefit in 2050 is 2.1 (95% CI: 2.04–2.18) Gt CO2, equivalent to 44.5% of China’s 2020 electricity sector emissions. In contrast, both national water and land saving exhibit a continuous upward trend through 2050 (Fig. 5b&c). By then, the national water saving is projected to reach 17 (95% CI: 16.5–17.4) km3, approximating 29.2% of the Yellow River’s groundwater reserves. The land saving will reach 289 thousand km2 (95% CI: 281–297), equivalent to about 18 times the administrative area of Beijing, and accounting for 20.1% of China’s planetary boundary for land-system change. This fundamental divergence underscores the evolving strategic value of rooftop PV, transitioning it from a primary climate mitigation tool in the near term to a crucial instrument for long-term water and land resource security.

Analysis of the top 20 GDP cities in 2050 reveals distinct tradeoffs between rooftop PV generation and its associated benefits (Fig. 5d). Beijing emerges as the strongest performer in co-benefits, achieving the highest water and land saving benefits nationwide, while Qingdao stands out for its exceptional carbon mitigation benefit. By contrast, Chongqing, despite hosting the largest rooftop PV generation potential, delivers only modest carbon, water, and land benefits, and Chengdu registers the lowest carbon mitigation among all major cities. Shanghai, although economically dominant, shows only moderate performance across all metrics. These contrasting patterns highlight that GDP scale does not necessarily translate into proportional PV co-benefits. To maximize national outcomes, urban PV deployment should follow differentiated strategies, expanding capacity in cities with both high potential and strong co-benefits, while offering targeted support and technological innovation in cities where benefits remain limited.

## Methods

City-level potential of rooftop photovoltaics
This study established a machine learning model to estimate the city-level rooftop PV potential for 349 Chinese cities for the baseline year of 2020. The model was trained using a rooftop PV area dataset18 derived from a 124-city analysis of individual buildings (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Notes). The 124-city baseline dataset was first disaggregated to the county level. This granular, county-level data was then used to train the machine learning model. After the model generated predictions for all counties nationwide, these results were re-aggregated to their respective city-level administrative boundaries to obtain the rooftop PV potential within built-up area in 2020 for all 349 cities. Our primary data collection effort then focused on compiling a set of city-level predictor variables for all target cities, including nighttime light, population, GDP, road length, and built-up area. The data sources, statistical characteristics and correlations of the variables are presented in Supplementary Table 9–10. To enhance model performance, we engineered additional features from this initial set, such as the ratio of urban area to GDP and road density. The LightGBM model was selected based on its performance in predicting the potential rooftop PV area. To handle the right-skewed distribution of the target variable, it was log-transformed prior to training. The model’s key hyperparameters, such as the maximum depth of the tree and the learning rate, were optimized using grid search techniques. The model performance and hyperparameters were assessed using a 10-fold cross-validation scheme applied to the county-level training samples, with the coefficient of determination (R2) as the primary evaluation metric and the L2 loss function (mean squared error, MSE) as the objective. The held-out fold in each split was used exclusively for evaluation and was not used for model fitting or hyperparameter selection, thereby minimizing information leakage during model development. The final LightGBM model achieved an R2 of 0.88 based on 10-fold cross-validation. To further examine the model’s stability, we conducted a stratified validation to assess its performance across China’s seven major geographical regions and different economic levels (Supplementary Fig. 2). The results indicate that the seven analyzed geographical regions exhibited R2 values above 0.83, ranging from 0.831 in Southwest China to 0.912 in Northern China (Supplementary Table 4). Additionally, it was revealed the stable predictive performance across different levels of economic development. When stratified into four tiers based on GDP (Low, Lower-Mid, Upper-Mid, and High), the model achieved R2 of 0.863, 0.872, 0.880, and 0.867, respectively (Supplementary Table 11). The mean absolute error (MAE) ranges from 0.045 km2 to 0.091 km2 and the root mean square error (RMSE) ranges from 0.389 km2 to 0.756 km2 across the quartiles.

To extend our predictions from the built-up area to the entire city administrative boundary, we implemented an LightGBM model, in a parallel process, to predict the total rooftop area within built-up areas, which achieved an R2 of 0.87 based on 10-fold cross-validation. We estimated total rooftop area in the surrounding hinterlands by subtracting the model-predicted total rooftop area of built-up areas from total rooftop area of entire city administrative boundaries11. Future scenario simulation
The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) are scenario frameworks for describing and analyzing future socio-economic development trends, which are mainly used for research in the fields of climate change, environment, resources, and policy, and are especially widely used in global climate change modelling61. The core purpose of SSP scenarios is to provide multiple socio-economic development pathways for climate change research and to help predict the impacts of climate change under different socio-economic development scenarios. To project the future rooftop PV potential, we employed a delta (change factor) method. This method scales our 2020 baseline potential based on the assumption that rooftop PV areas grow proportionally to the total rooftop areas. The future projections for global rooftop area were sourced from Joshi et al.62, where the data were generated using a machine learning model driven by SSP-specific factors. As the surface-downwelling shortwave radiation is the main cause of the variability in solar power generation, we computed average annual rooftop PV power generation using daily estimates of surface-downwelling shortwave radiation rendered by GCMs from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 6 (CMIP6). The data are obtained from the World Climate Research Program’s Working Group. By combining the five SSPs with these three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs)—RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5, our study evaluates a matrix of 15 future SSP-RCP scenarios. This combination follows the standard design of the CMIP6 framework and was deliberately chosen to systematically explore a wide range of plausible futures. We note that our analysis does not cover all possible variants, such as SSP370, which represents a future of heightened regional rivalry, and the exploration of which is beyond the scope of this study. Our scenario framework encompasses a spectrum from a sustainable, stringent mitigation future aligned with the Paris Agreement (e.g., SSP126), to a middle-of-the-road trajectory (e.g., SSP245), and a high-emission, fossil-fueled development pathway (e.g., SSP585). Within this framework, scenarios such as SSP126 and SSP245 are particularly relevant to China’s policy context and long-term carbon neutrality goals. The delta downscaling method (deviation-corrected change factor method) was further used to correct SSP and RCP scenario data from 2025 to 2050. To represent the future evolution of provincial power generation mix, we adopted optimized generation structures for 2025–2050 derived from a province-level energy modeling framework63. Based on the dynamic mixes, we calculated the carbon, water, and land intensities of provincial power generation. The assessment covered a full portfolio of generation technologies, including coal, gas, biomass, hydro, wind, solar, and nuclear power. In our research, with a specific focus on wind and solar as the key drivers of decarbonization, the onshore wind and utility-scale PV in the power mix were selected as the representative technologies to reflect technological advancement, while the life cycle intensities of other generation technologies were held constant. To be specific, we estimated the future annual generation of wind and utility-scale PV based on technology-specific drivers (improving capacity factors for wind64, and changing solar radiation and conversion efficiency for PV). We further updated the future life cycle inventories of wind and utility-scale PV, including embodied material impact decrease and recycling rate increase. See Supplementary Fig. 14 for the details.

Concurrently, we developed a dynamic life cycle inventory framework specifically for rooftop PV systems to simulate the distinct technological trajectories. Key assumptions were as follows: recycling rates for major module materials (limestone, soda, silica sand, copper, and aluminum) were assumed to increase at a conservative annual rate of 2%, reflecting progressive material recovery policies; the embodied environmental intensities of non-electrical components, including glass, aluminum frames, and mounting brackets, were assumed to decline by 1% per year, representing cleaner material production65; PV module degradation was incorporated, with a rate of 2% in the first year and 0.55% annually thereafter, based on field investigation; and PV module conversion efficiency was projected to improve at an annual rate of 0.35%, starting from a 2020 baseline of 16%, according to the Energy Research Institute of the National Development and Reform Commission of China66. Notably, throughout the whole life cycle, the electricity for rooftop PV comes from the evolving provincial power generation mix from 2025 to 2050. To capture parametric uncertainties, we also implemented a Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations) on critical variables, including cleaning water usage, solar irradiation, and provincial grid mix.

We further evaluated future rooftop PV deployment schemes that incorporate economic feasibility to reflect realistic deployment constraints. Specifically, the 349 cities were ranked by their LCOE from low to high and divided into four quartiles. Development rates of 80%, 60%, 30%, and 10% were assigned to the first through fourth quartiles, respectively, capturing the decreasing likelihood of deployment with lower economic attractiveness. The economically adjusted rooftop PV potential for each city and SSP pathway was then calculated by multiplying the maximum technical potential by the corresponding development rate. Based on the city-level rooftop PV deployment schemes, we quantified the future carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV. Simulation results are reported using the median (50th percentile) as the central estimate, with 95% confidence intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) provided to characterize the uncertainty bounds. To further evaluate the broader significance of the carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV, we benchmarked them against China’s national shares of planetary boundaries67, thereby assessing the extent to which rooftop PV can contribute to mitigating environmental pressures within safe operating limits.

## Paper

## Abstract

Rooftop photovoltaics are widely recognized for their carbon mitigation benefits, yet uncertainties persist regarding their future dynamics and broader impacts on water and land. Here we develop a city-level integrated framework to quantify rooftop photovoltaics potential across 349 Chinese cities, and evaluate evolving carbon-water-land tradeoffs under shared socioeconomic and representative concentration pathways. By 2050, projections across 15 combined scenarios indicate China’s rooftop photovoltaic areas will increase by 9.2 to 34.8 percent relative to 2020 levels. Installed capacity ranges from 7.19 to 9.05 terawatts in 2050, expanding rapidly in eastern coastal cities. Under a moderate socioeconomic and climate scenario, the national carbon mitigation benefits peak during 2035 to 2040, accumulating 2.04 to 2.18 gigatons of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2050. In contrast, the water and land saving benefits continue to rise, reaching 16.5 to 17.4 cubic kilometers and 281 to 297 thousand square kilometers by 2050. These findings underscore the critical need for multidimensional planning to optimize future sustainable photovoltaics deployment.

---

## Introduction

Cities are pivotal engines of future population growth, innovation, and economic opportunity worldwide1. Yet, a significant share of global urban areas still faces acute energy shortages, with approximately 760 million people globally lacking access to electricity in 2023, predominantly in developing countries and emerging economies2. Conventional power generation systems, often located far from demand centers3, thus remain out of sight and mind for the public. Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems, a hallmark of distributed energy, utilize idle urban rooftop spaces to enable localized power generation4, which can offer remarkable spatial adaptability and energy self-sufficiency5,6. Compared with centralized power plants, rooftop PV not only reduces long-distance transmission losses by an estimated 6–8%7 but minimizes land requirements, making it an effective strategy for alleviating urban land use conflicts and enhancing the resilience of energy systems8,9. Globally, the development potential of rooftop resources is vast. Estimates suggest that rooftops cover 200,000 km2 of the planet’s 13 million km2 land surface, with Asia accounting for a substantial share10. In China alone, the total rooftop area across 354 cities reached 66,000 km2 by 2020, signaling enormous untapped capacity for rooftop PV deployment11.

Amid intensifying global warming, the carbon mitigation benefits of rooftop PV have garnered widespread attention12. Research has largely centered on carbon emission mitigation during the operational phase13–18. Yet recent insights suggest that ignoring emissions across the full life cycle—from raw material extraction through manufacturing, transport, installation, and maintenance—may inflate the perceived climate benefits of rooftop PV19–22. Moreover, a singular focus on carbon mitigation may obscure the multidimensional impacts of rooftop PV and miss opportunities to embrace broader sustainability development goal (SDG). Recognizing the close interlinkages between energy (SDG7), carbon (SDG13), water (SDG6), and land (SDG15)23,24, urban policymakers should integrate a holistic view that considers not just energy generation, but also the indirect resource consumption (e.g., materials) and its cascading implications for water and land systems25.

In terms of water use, though rooftop PV consumes water during material production and operation26,27, its life cycle water footprint remains lower than that of fossil fuel-based generation mix. In California, for example, residential rooftop PV saves an average of 200 cubic meters of water annually, around 60% of the typical American household’s consumption28. Regarding direct land use, rooftop PV capitalizes on existing urban building landscapes, and avoids the need for additional ground space29,30. While utility-scale PV stations conversely depend on vast tracts of farmland, grassland, or ecological zones, potentially triggering land use conflicts and ecological pressures31–33. Coal-based power compounds this issue with extensive land demands for mining, storage, and transmission34. Seen from the entire lifespan, rooftop PV entails indirect land occupation that amounts to only a fraction of that associated with coal-fired power26,35. Nevertheless, whether rooftop PV consistently offers land saving advantages over power generation mix warrants further quantification.

As ambitious calls for net-zero power systems grow, the large-scale integration of renewables promises to sharply lower carbon emission factors of power generation mix36–38. However, the carbon mitigation benefit of rooftop PV will inherently change, when considering the generation mix decarbonizes and rooftop PV’s technological advancement. Meanwhile, little is known about the future performance of rooftop PV regarding water and land dimensions. These uncertainties complicate efforts to evaluate the energy-carbon-water-land tradeoffs between rooftop PV and power generation mix, particularly under varying future socio-economic-climate trajectories. Bridging these knowledge gaps can help refine contributions of rooftop PV to the SDGs and inform tailored, evidence-based urban energy strategies.

To tackle these challenges, we constructed a city-level methodological framework for quantifying the rooftop PV’s tradeoffs (Fig. 1), blending machine learning, life cycle assessment, and forward-looking scenario simulations. The model can map out city-level rooftop PV potential and quantify the associated carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving, projecting their evolutionary trends from 2025 to 2050. By weaving in socio-economic-climate scenarios, provincial generation mix evolution, and PV technological advancement from 2025 onward, we illuminate the nexus dynamics of rooftop PV across multiple dimensions. Applied to 349 Chinese cities, we uncover the notable spatial variations of rooftop PV in tradeoffs against local power generation mix. This study equips stakeholders with a view of rooftop PV’s untapped value and arms urban decision-makers with context-specific evidence for designing effective, locally tailored energy transitions.

---

## Results

Rooftop photovoltaic potential within city boundaries
This study developed a machine learning model to predict the rooftop PV potential across 349 Chinese cities, including built-up areas and hinterlands within city administrative boundaries. To assess the robustness and generalizability, the cross-validation procedure was applied to subsets of data stratified by China’s seven geographical regions and by city-level gross domestic product (GDP) classifications (see Methods and Supplementary Figs. 1–2). We estimated that China possesses a total of 33,290 km2 of rooftop PV potential across 349 cities. However, this resource is distributed unevenly, with the majority located in densely built and highly urbanized eastern regions. At the city scale, rooftop PV potential varies substantially, ranging from 2.4 km2 in Wuzhishan to 533 km2 in Chongqing. The leading cities include Chongqing, Weifang, Linyi, Shijiazhuang, and Baoding (Fig. 2a). Comparing built-up areas to hinterlands, Shenzhen, Shantou, and Wuzhishan offer higher rooftop PV potential in built-up areas. While the other 99% of cities exhibit greater potential in hinterlands, ranging from 1.2 to 68 times higher than built-up areas, which is consistent across all provinces (Supplementary Fig. 6). Shandong province exemplifies this spatial structure, as its extensive rooftop areas in hinterlands, combined with strong policy support, have enabled it to emerge as a national leader in distributed rooftop PV development.

We compared the rooftop PV generation with total electricity demand in city administrative boundaries (Supplementary Fig. 7) to evaluate the theoretical urban electricity self-sufficiency (UESS). The UESS ranges from 16% to 417% (Supplementary Fig. 8a). It was further found that 87% of cities (302 of 349), primarily concentrated east of the Hu Huanyong Line (Fig. 2b), could theoretically generate more electricity than they consume. In built-up areas, rooftop PV can meet a small portion of demand, ranging from 0.8% to 58.5% (Fig. 2c). Conversely, rooftop PV in hinterland can satisfy 11%–403% of city electricity demand (Fig. 2d), and 82% of cities (286 of 349) can fully achieve the electricity self-sufficiency.

Our assessment of China’s five largest cities by GDP (Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Chongqing, and Guangzhou) shows significant variation in the potential for rooftop PV to meet local electricity demand (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Among them, Chongqing exhibits the greatest theoretical self-sufficiency (134.5%), with generation capacity far exceeding its demand. This is largely driven by its hinterland (126.8%), while its built-up area contributes only 7.7%. In contrast, Shenzhen (53.8% total) follows a built-up area–dominated mode, where 40.1% of potential arises from the urban core compared to only 13.7% from the hinterland, consistent with its compact urban form. For Shanghai, Beijing, and Guangzhou, they rely significantly on their hinterlands. Shanghai has a total UESS of 58.2%, with 41.0% coming from the hinterland and 17.2% from the built-up area. In Beijing and Guangzhou, built-up areas contribute around 18.5% and 12.8%, respectively, to their total UESS, while the hinterlands provide the larger share. These profiles underscore the importance of aligning rooftop PV deployment strategies with the spatial configurations and morphological characteristics of different megacities.

Energy-carbon-water-land nexus of rooftop photovoltaics
By integrating local solar irradiation, PV conversion efficiency, and performance ratio, we evaluated the rooftop PV generation potential across cities (Fig. 3a). Since rooftop PV systems offer a viable alternative to local power generation mix, the comparison between rooftop PV and generation mix is crucial to determine the practical benefits and limitations of each. We defined the life cycle system boundaries for rooftop PV, encompassing material production, manufacturing, transportation, installation, operation, decommissioning, disposal, and recycling (Supplementary Fig. 9). We included the direct impacts (energy and water input, carbon emissions), and accounted for the embodied impacts (by materials and resources) of rooftop PV (Supplementary Methods). In particular, we incorporated the direct cleaning water usage during operational stage, informed by company interviews on rooftop PV practices (Supplementary Table 2), which cover diverse techniques (e.g., robots, drones, handheld brushes) with varying water intensities and cleaning frequencies. The life cycle assessment results per kilowatt-hour (kWh) indicate that rooftop PV systems generate carbon emissions (52.2–99.3 g kWh-1), and require water consumption (0.34–0.65 L kWh-1) as well as land occupation (0.0034–0.0064 m2 kWh-1). For comparison, we benchmarked the life cycle impacts of rooftop PV against the local power generation mix on a per kWh electricity basis. The life cycle carbon emission, water consumption, and land occupation of power generation mix (Supplementary Table 5) were computed based on provincial generation structures (Supplementary Table 6) and the corresponding life cycle impacts of each generation technology (see Methods for details). Our analysis reveals that rooftop PV substantially outperforms generation mix across the carbon, water, and land impact dimensions from a life cycle perspective. Specifically, for each kWh of electricity generated compared with generation mix, city-level rooftop PV in China provides median benefits of 759 g in carbon mitigation, 3.4 L in water saving, and 0.05 m2 in land saving. These benefits exhibit significant spatial heterogeneity, with city-level values ranging from 81.6–1362 g kWh-1 for carbon mitigation, 2.4–15.1 L kWh-1 for water saving, and 0.02–0.11 m2 kWh-1 for land saving.

From a carbon perspective, rooftop PV generation in provinces such as Inner Mongolia (1348–1362 g kWh-1), Jilin (1070–1076 g kWh-1), Heilongjiang (1064–1074 g kWh-1), Shanxi (1041–1049 g kWh-1), and Zhejiang (1041–1046 g kWh-1) showcase high carbon mitigation benefits (Fig. 3b). This is primarily due to the high proportion of coal power in the power structures of these provinces and the high life cycle carbon intensity of coal power generation. However, regions like Sichuan (82–124 g kWh-1) and Yunnan (100–121 g kWh-1) exhibit poor carbon mitigation benefits (Fig. 3b) and long carbon payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3a). The main reasons for this are twofold: First, these areas benefit from low-carbon generation structures dominated by hydropower, indicating that the electricity substituted by rooftop PV is already clean, which results in minimal mitigation. Second, weak solar radiation (especially for some cities in Sichuan) due to basin topography reduces the lifetime energy generation of PV systems. This effectively increases the PV system’s life cycle carbon emissions per kWh generation, diminishing its overall life cycle environmental benefits. However, Sichuan (14.9–15.1 L kWh-1), Yunnan (14.3–14.3 L kWh-1), Qinghai (11.3–11.34 L kWh-1), and Hubei (10.5–10.6 L kWh-1) exhibit the most substantial water saving benefits through rooftop PV generation (Fig. 3c), leading to the lowest water payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3b). This is because their provincial generation mixes contain a high share of hydropower, whose life cycle water consumption is comparatively large, thereby leading to greater water saving when substituted by rooftop PV. Heilongjiang and Hainan stand out for their substantial land saving benefits, with values of 0.105–0.106 m2 kWh-1 and 0.962–0.967 m2 kWh-1, respectively (Fig. 3d). This stems from the higher proportion of biomass in the power structure of these two provinces. Biomass has a greater life cycle land occupation, and thus elevate the land factors of generation mix. The rooftop PV in these regions thereby yields more pronounced land saving benefits, resulting in shorter land payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3c). Conversely, Qinghai (0.023–0.024 m2 kWh-1), Shaanxi (0.033–0.035 m2 kWh-1), Guizhou (0.033–0.034 m2 kWh-1), Xinjiang (0.028–0.029 m2 kWh-1), and Gansu (0.0275–0.0289 m2 kWh-1) present the least significant land saving benefit (Fig. 3d) and, therefore, have longer land payback periods (Supplementary Fig. 3c).

Beyond resource and environmental impacts, we evaluated the economic performance of urban rooftop PV using the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), explicitly accounting for rooftop rental costs (Supplementary Table 7) in addition to initial capital investment, operation and maintenance costs. The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of rooftop PV is estimated at 0.041–0.077 USD kWh-1 (Fig. 3e), ensuring user-side grid parity across 349 cities (Supplementary Fig. 5), that is, rooftop PV electricity costs are no higher than the retail tariffs paid by consumers. The payback periods, however, exhibit pronounced heterogeneity (Supplementary Fig. 3d), mainly driven by differences in local electricity tariffs, rooftop rents as well as PV generation. Due to low electricity tariff in Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, and low generation per unit area in Sichuan, Guizhou, and Gansu, Xinjiang (13.8–16.9 years), Inner Mongolia (11–14.5 years), Sichuan (8.4–16.2 years), Guizhou (12.9–16.9 years), Gansu (11.1–16.6 years), and parts of Shaanxi (9.7–14.4 years) require longer periods to offset their economic costs. We further examined the spatial distribution of the economic cost required per unit of benefit (based on the normalized sum of carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving) for urban rooftop PV (Fig. 3f). Gansu, Shaanxi, Guizhou, Fujian, and Guangdong challenge high costs when generating carbon-water-land benefits, while Heilongjiang, Jilin, Hebei, Yunnan, and parts of Inner Mongolia and Sichuan have low costs, driven by favorable LCOE and positive environmental performances in carbon mitigation, water saving, and land saving. These heterogeneities suggest that deployment strategies should be tailored to specific regions. Areas with high benefits and low costs should prioritize the adoption of rooftop PV, while regions with high costs require policy and technological support to enhance the viability of deploying urban rooftop PV.

Future scenarios reshape rooftop photovoltaics’ nexus
Under the framework of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), we projected the expansion of China’s rooftop PV area from 2025 to 2050, based on the maximum exploitable potential. Our results indicate substantial variations in future rooftop PV expansion, with growth trajectories diverging markedly among SSPs. By 2050, the fossil-fueled development scenario (SSP5) shows the largest increase, with the national rooftop PV area reaching a median of 44,877 km2, representing a 34.8% rise (95% CI: 31.9%–37.5%) relative to 2020 levels. In contrast, the sustainability scenario (SSP1) yields the smallest increase, reaching 36,346 km2, and a 9.2% rise (95% CI: 7.3%–11.1%). The intermediate scenarios fall between these two extremes: the middle-of-the-road scenario (SSP2) results in a 24.8% increase (95% CI: 22.2%–27.3%), while the regional rivalry (SSP3) and inequality (SSP4) scenarios show moderate growth of 14.9% (95% CI: 12.3%–17.5%) and 14.5% (95% CI: 12.1%–17.1%), respectively (Fig. 4a).

We further combined the SSP-based rooftop PV area projections with radiative forcing estimates under three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs), including RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5. This integration enabled Monte Carlo simulations of China’s rooftop PV installed capacity potential from 2025 to 2050, covering 15 SSP–RCP combinations. Under the maximum rooftop PV potential, the median national installed capacity by 2050 is projected to increase by 74.4% (95% CI: 67.3%–81.6%) under the SSP185 scenario and by 119.6% (95% CI: 98.6%–141.2%) under the SSP545 scenario, corresponding to 7.19 TW (95% CI: 6.89–7.49 TW) and 9.05 TW (95% CI: 8.19–9.92 TW), respectively (Fig. 4b). Under the middle-of-the-road SSP245 pathway, the national installed capacity will to reach a median of 8.2 TW by 2050, a 103% increase (95% CI: 87.4%–119.4%) relative to year 2020 (Fig. 4b). Under the SSP245 scenario, rooftop PV generation across China’s 349 cities will increase substantially, with the national average growth reaching 87.5% by 2030 and 193.6% by 2050 relative to 2020 levels (Fig. 4c). However, this potential is highly uneven, the eastern coastal cities are primary hotspots for future rooftop PV deployment, with Shandong projected to reach 786.7 GW by 2050 (Supplementary Table 8). A broad cohort of economically developed cities or those with abundant solar resources in this region, including Huizhou, Wenzhou, Ningde, and Qingdao, consistently exhibit strong long-term potential, with projected growth rates commonly exceeding 200%. In addition, cities like Panjin (448.8%), Mianyang (406.5%), and Longyan (347.9%) are projected to see their generation increase more than four-fold, indicating significant local drivers. Whereas cities in the northwest or less-developed regions, such as Jiayuguan and Wuzhishan, show significantly more modest, though still positive, growth trajectories.

We incorporated anticipated advances in rooftop PV to project the future life cycle carbon, water, and land intensities of rooftop PV systems, including improved conversion efficiency, enhanced recycling rate, and decreased embodied impacts of key materials. These life cycle evolution of rooftop PV was integrated with provincial power generation structure optimization scenarios to assess the future dynamics among carbon, water, and land benefits. Under policy-driven constraints, coal- and gas-fired generation in the power structure is projected to peak around 2030 and 2040, respectively, while renewable penetration increases, with solar and wind power progressively dominating China’s electricity mix, complemented by hydropower, nuclear, and biomass (Supplementary Fig. 10). Within the power generation mix, the life cycle carbon, water, and land intensities of solar and wind power are projected to evolve over time, reflecting anticipated technological advancement, and the intensities of other generation technologies (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, and biomass) are assumed constant. The results indicate that the life cycle carbon intensity of rooftop PV steadily decreases with technological advancement, and the carbon intensities of power generation mix also decline due to a rising share of renewables (Supplementary Fig. 11). For water and land, however, the trajectories of provincial generation mix factors are more heterogeneous. Some provinces exhibit decreases, whereas others remain relatively stable or fluctuate depending on their generation structure (Supplementary Fig. 11). In contrast, rooftop PV shows a consistent downward trend in water and land intensities. These dynamics highlight that the relative benefits of rooftop PV are shaped jointly by PV technological advancement and generation structure evolution differences. Results show that the unit carbon mitigation benefit is projected to decrease over time, with the median value declining from 713.6 g kWh-1 in 2025 to 388 g kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). Similarly, the unit water saving benefit shows a slight downward trend, with the median decreasing from 3.9 L kWh-1 in 2025 to 3.5 L kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12b). In contrast, the unit land saving benefit demonstrates an increase, rising from 0.043 m2 kWh-1 in 2025 to 0.056 m2 kWh-1 in 2050 (Supplementary Fig. 12c), with the growing efficiency of life cycle land occupation of rooftop PV. The unit benefits and payback periods, with and without technological advancements, are additionally shown in Supplementary Fig. 12d–f.

We further developed economically-constrained deployment scenarios to reflect the possibilities of market attractiveness on city-level rooftop PV rollout. To achieve this, we ranked and grouped all 349 cities into four quartiles based on their LCOE. We then applied tiered deployment rates to these quartiles to simulate a market-driven pathway where more profitable regions are prioritized. Specifically, the deployment rates were set at 80%, 60%, 30%, and 10%, corresponding to the quartiles from the most economically attractive (lowest LCOE) to the least. The final deployment level for each city under a given SSP scenario was then determined by multiplying its maximum technical potential by its assigned quartile-specific rate. This approach allows for the evaluation of future carbon, water, and land benefits under large-scale rooftop PV development schemes. Results show that at the national scale, the carbon mitigation benefit of rooftop PV will first rise to a peak around 2035–2040 and then decline (Fig. 5a), while the water and land saving benefits will consistently increase over time (Fig. 5b&c). Under the SSP245 scenario, the carbon mitigation benefit in 2050 is 2.1 (95% CI: 2.04–2.18) Gt CO2, equivalent to 44.5% of China’s 2020 electricity sector emissions. In contrast, both national water and land saving exhibit a continuous upward trend through 2050 (Fig. 5b&c). By then, the national water saving is projected to reach 17 (95% CI: 16.5–17.4) km3, approximating 29.2% of the Yellow River’s groundwater reserves. The land saving will reach 289 thousand km2 (95% CI: 281–297), equivalent to about 18 times the administrative area of Beijing, and accounting for 20.1% of China’s planetary boundary for land-system change. This fundamental divergence underscores the evolving strategic value of rooftop PV, transitioning it from a primary climate mitigation tool in the near term to a crucial instrument for long-term water and land resource security.

Analysis of the top 20 GDP cities in 2050 reveals distinct tradeoffs between rooftop PV generation and its associated benefits (Fig. 5d). Beijing emerges as the strongest performer in co-benefits, achieving the highest water and land saving benefits nationwide, while Qingdao stands out for its exceptional carbon mitigation benefit. By contrast, Chongqing, despite hosting the largest rooftop PV generation potential, delivers only modest carbon, water, and land benefits, and Chengdu registers the lowest carbon mitigation among all major cities. Shanghai, although economically dominant, shows only moderate performance across all metrics. These contrasting patterns highlight that GDP scale does not necessarily translate into proportional PV co-benefits. To maximize national outcomes, urban PV deployment should follow differentiated strategies, expanding capacity in cities with both high potential and strong co-benefits, while offering targeted support and technological innovation in cities where benefits remain limited.

---

## Methods

City-level potential of rooftop photovoltaics
This study established a machine learning model to estimate the city-level rooftop PV potential for 349 Chinese cities for the baseline year of 2020. The model was trained using a rooftop PV area dataset18 derived from a 124-city analysis of individual buildings (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Notes). The 124-city baseline dataset was first disaggregated to the county level. This granular, county-level data was then used to train the machine learning model. After the model generated predictions for all counties nationwide, these results were re-aggregated to their respective city-level administrative boundaries to obtain the rooftop PV potential within built-up area in 2020 for all 349 cities. Our primary data collection effort then focused on compiling a set of city-level predictor variables for all target cities, including nighttime light, population, GDP, road length, and built-up area. The data sources, statistical characteristics and correlations of the variables are presented in Supplementary Table 9–10. To enhance model performance, we engineered additional features from this initial set, such as the ratio of urban area to GDP and road density. The LightGBM model was selected based on its performance in predicting the potential rooftop PV area. To handle the right-skewed distribution of the target variable, it was log-transformed prior to training. The model’s key hyperparameters, such as the maximum depth of the tree and the learning rate, were optimized using grid search techniques. The model performance and hyperparameters were assessed using a 10-fold cross-validation scheme applied to the county-level training samples, with the coefficient of determination (R2) as the primary evaluation metric and the L2 loss function (mean squared error, MSE) as the objective. The held-out fold in each split was used exclusively for evaluation and was not used for model fitting or hyperparameter selection, thereby minimizing information leakage during model development. The final LightGBM model achieved an R2 of 0.88 based on 10-fold cross-validation. Future scenario simulation
The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) are scenario frameworks for describing and analyzing future socio-economic development trends, which are mainly used for research in the fields of climate change, environment, resources, and policy, and are especially widely used in global climate change modelling61. The core purpose of SSP scenarios is to provide multiple socio-economic development pathways for climate change research and to help predict the impacts of climate change under different socio-economic development scenarios. To project the future rooftop PV potential, we employed a delta (change factor) method. This method scales our 2020 baseline potential based on the assumption that rooftop PV areas grow proportionally to the total rooftop areas. The future projections for global rooftop area were sourced from Joshi et al.62, where the data were generated using a machine learning model driven by SSP-specific factors. As the surface-downwelling shortwave radiation is the main cause of the variability in solar power generation, we computed average annual rooftop PV power generation using daily estimates of surface-downwelling shortwave radiation rendered by GCMs from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 6 (CMIP6). The data are obtained from the World Climate Research Program’s Working Group. By combining the five SSPs with these three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs)—RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5, our study evaluates a matrix of 15 future SSP-RCP scenarios. This combination follows the standard design of the CMIP6 framework and was deliberately chosen to systematically explore a wide range of plausible futures. We note that our analysis does not cover all possible variants, such as SSP370, which represents a future of heightened regional rivalry, and the exploration of which is beyond the scope of this study. Our scenario framework encompasses a spectrum from a sustainable, stringent mitigation future aligned with the Paris Agreement (e.g., SSP126), to a middle-of-the-road trajectory (e.g., SSP245), and a high-emission, fossil-fueled development pathway (e.g., SSP585). Within this framework, scenarios such as SSP126 and SSP245 are particularly relevant to China’s policy context and long-term carbon neutrality goals. To represent the future evolution of provincial power generation mix, we adopted optimized generation structures for 2025–2050 derived from a province-level energy modeling framework63. Based on the dynamic mixes, we calculated the carbon, water, and land intensities of provincial power generation. The assessment covered a full portfolio of generation technologies, including coal, gas, biomass, hydro, wind, solar, and nuclear power. In our research, with a specific focus on wind and solar as the key drivers of decarbonization, the onshore wind and utility-scale PV in the power mix were selected as the representative technologies to reflect technological advancement, while the life cycle intensities of other generation technologies were held constant. To be specific, we estimated the future annual generation of wind and utility-scale PV based on technology-specific drivers (improving capacity factors for wind64, and changing solar radiation and conversion efficiency for PV). We further updated the future life cycle inventories of wind and utility-scale PV, including embodied material impact decrease and recycling rate increase. See Supplementary Fig. 14 for the details.

Concurrently, we developed a dynamic life cycle inventory framework specifically for rooftop PV systems to simulate the distinct technological trajectories. Key assumptions were as follows: recycling rates for major module materials (limestone, soda, silica sand, copper, and aluminum) were assumed to increase at a conservative annual rate of 2%, reflecting progressive material recovery policies; the embodied environmental intensities of non-electrical components, including glass, aluminum frames, and mounting brackets, were assumed to decline by 1% per year, representing cleaner material production65; PV module degradation was incorporated, with a rate of 2% in the first year and 0.55% annually thereafter, based on field investigation; and PV module conversion efficiency was projected to improve at an annual rate of 0.35%, starting from a 2020 baseline of 16%, according to the Energy Research Institute of the National Development and Reform Commission of China66. Notably, throughout the whole life cycle, the electricity for rooftop PV comes from the evolving provincial power generation mix from 2025 to 2050. To capture parametric uncertainties, we also implemented a Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 iterations) on critical variables, including cleaning water usage, solar irradiation, and provincial grid mix.

We further evaluated future rooftop PV deployment schemes that incorporate economic feasibility to reflect realistic deployment constraints. Specifically, the 349 cities were ranked by their LCOE from low to high and divided into four quartiles. Development rates of 80%, 60%, 30%, and 10% were assigned to the first through fourth quartiles, respectively, capturing the decreasing likelihood of deployment with lower economic attractiveness. The economically adjusted rooftop PV potential for each city and SSP pathway was then calculated by multiplying the maximum technical potential by the corresponding development rate. Based on the city-level rooftop PV deployment schemes, we quantified the future carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV. Simulation results are reported using the median (50th percentile) as the central estimate, with 95% confidence intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) provided to characterize the uncertainty bounds. To further evaluate the broader significance of the carbon, water, and land benefits of rooftop PV, we benchmarked them against China’s national shares of planetary boundaries67, thereby assessing the extent to which rooftop PV can contribute to mitigating environmental pressures within safe operating limits.

consistent with the resolution of available official data (e.g., from the Ministry of

the provincial level. Distributed PV generation within a city displaces electricity
